title: GOD COMMANDED AN ENTIRE NATION TO CURSE THESE SINS OUT LOUD—BUT WHAT HAPPENS WHEN THE GUILTY PERSON IS SOMEONE YOU LOVE?
paragraphs: GOD COMMANDED AN ENTIRE NATION TO CURSE THESE SINS OUT LOUD—BUT WHAT HAPPENS WHEN THE GUILTY PERSON IS SOMEONE YOU LOVE?

The terrifying public declarations of Deuteronomy 27:20–23 reveal why God refuses to call sexual betrayal a private matter—and why the same Bible that exposes hidden sin ultimately leads us to the cross, where Jesus Christ offers forgiveness, justice, and the possibility of a completely different ending.
There are sins people confess.
And there are sins families bury.

Some are hidden behind locked doors. Some behind respected surnames. Some behind Sunday clothes, polished reputations, and photographs of smiling relatives who have learned never to mention what happened.
Sometimes everyone knows.
But nobody speaks.
The victim is told to move on. The offender is protected because of his position. The family reputation becomes more important than the wounded person. And silence is renamed peace.
Then you open the Bible.
And suddenly, you encounter something almost impossible to imagine.
God commanded an entire nation to stand together and publicly pronounce curses against certain sexual violations committed within the family.
Not whisper about them.
Not excuse them because the offender was influential.
Not pretend they were harmless because they happened behind closed doors.
Publicly declare them.
And the people were commanded to answer:
“Amen.”
Think about that.

The very God who would later reveal the fullness of His mercy in Jesus Christ also required His covenant people to acknowledge, in public, that certain hidden acts were utterly unacceptable before Him.
Why?
Why would the God of love demand such a solemn declaration?
And what does that mean for someone who has committed a shameful sin, someone who has been wounded by another person's sin, or someone who has spent years pretending that nothing happened?
Stay with this, because the answer is not simply about ancient Israel.
It is about holiness.
It is about the danger of protecting evil with silence.
And, ultimately, it is about a Savior who does not need to deny the seriousness of sin in order to rescue sinners.
In Deuteronomy 27, Moses instructed Israel concerning a covenant ceremony to take place after the people entered the land God had promised them.

Six tribes were to stand on Mount Gerizim in connection with the blessing, and six on Mount Ebal in connection with the curse. The Levites would pronounce solemn covenant declarations, and the people would respond.
This was not a spectacle invented to humiliate selected individuals. It was a national acknowledgment of the moral obligations of God's covenant.
Israel was being taught that obedience to God could not be separated from the way people treated one another, including those within their own households.
Then came words that should still make us tremble.
Deuteronomy 27:20 declares in the King James Version:
“Cursed be he that lieth with his father's wife; because he uncovereth his father's skirt. And all the people shall say, Amen.”
The Hebrew begins:
אָרוּר שֹׁכֵב עִם־אֵשֶׁת אָבִיו
Arur shokhev im-eshet aviv.
Meaning, in context:
“Cursed is the one who lies with his father's wife.”
The word אָרוּר (arur) means “cursed.” It is a solemn declaration of covenant judgment, not an invitation for the crowd to unleash personal revenge.

The expression translated “his father's wife” is significant. It identifies a woman through her marital relationship to the man's father. This prohibition includes a stepmother and should not be reduced merely to the biological mother-son relationship.
The verse goes further by explaining that the act dishonors the father's marital relationship and violates the boundaries God established.
This is not simply about an ancient society being uncomfortable with an unconventional relationship.
It is about a fundamental betrayal of family boundaries.
And the congregation was required to say, “Amen.”
In Hebrew:
אָמֵן (amen).
The word expresses affirmation—something like “truly,” or “so be it.”
Imagine standing among thousands of people and hearing the declaration.
You could not pretend that God had never spoken.
You could not honestly say that family relationships were morally unimportant.
You were being called to affirm that God's judgment was right.
Then came another declaration.
Deuteronomy 27:22:
“Cursed be he that lieth with his sister, the daughter of his father, or the daughter of his mother. And all the people shall say, Amen.”
The Hebrew expression אֲחֹתוֹ (achoto) means “his sister.”
The wording expressly includes a sister through either parent, covering the relevant half-sibling relationships as well.
This prohibition was not based on whether the relationship could be kept secret.
It was not suspended because two people claimed they had developed feelings.
It was not erased because nobody outside the household knew.
God's moral boundaries were not determined by the likelihood of discovery.
And again, the people answered:
“Amen.”
Then Deuteronomy 27:23:
“Cursed be he that lieth with his mother in law. And all the people shall say, Amen.”
The Hebrew word חֹתַנְתּוֹ (chotanto) refers to his mother-in-law.
Once again, the command addresses sexual conduct that violates an established family relationship.
The passage also includes another prohibition that must not be overlooked.
Deuteronomy 27:21 declares:
“Cursed be he that lieth with any manner of beast. And all the people shall say, Amen.”
This verse concerns bestiality, not incest. It appears within the same sequence of public declarations and shows that the passage addresses more than one category of forbidden sexual behavior.
The Bible is specific.
And when we speak about Scripture, we must be specific too.
Deuteronomy 27:20–23 does not describe a public trial of named offenders, nor does it command Israel to parade victims before a crowd.
It commands a public affirmation of covenant standards.
That distinction matters.
Because God's Word must never be twisted into permission to publicly expose, mock, or retraumatize people who have already suffered abuse.
The purpose of the declarations was to establish that these acts were morally forbidden before God, even when committed in private.
And that raises a painful question.
What happens when the people who should protect a family become the very people who violate its sacred boundaries?
For some readers, this is not an abstract theological discussion.
You remember the room.
The voice.
The threat.
The warning not to tell anybody.
Maybe you were too young to understand what was happening. Maybe you understood enough to feel frightened, but not enough to know how to ask for help.
Maybe the person responsible was someone everyone respected.
A relative.
A trusted adult.
Someone whose public reputation made your private experience almost impossible to explain.
And perhaps, when you finally tried to speak, somebody told you that exposing the truth would destroy the family.
But listen carefully.
The person who reveals abuse is not the person who created it.
The responsibility belongs to the person who committed the wrong.
If you were abused, coerced, threatened, or exploited, the shame of that wrongdoing does not belong to you.
And no appeal to forgiveness, family loyalty, religious reputation, or submission should ever be used to force you back into danger.
God's holiness is not an excuse for cruelty toward victims.
It is one of the reasons wrongdoing must be taken seriously.
That is why the wider context of Deuteronomy matters.
Only a few verses earlier, Deuteronomy 27:19 declares a curse against anyone who perverts justice for the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow.
The same covenant ceremony that condemned forbidden sexual acts also condemned injustice toward vulnerable people.
God was not merely concerned with maintaining appearances.
He was concerned with righteousness.
And righteousness cannot flourish where the powerful are protected while the wounded are silenced.
But now we must confront another truth.
Not everyone reading this is identifying with the victim.
Some are remembering a sin they committed.
A boundary they crossed.
A relationship they knew was forbidden.
A secret they have defended for years.
Perhaps nobody knows.
Perhaps you have become skilled at keeping your outward life separate from the things you have done.
You still attend church.
You still know the songs.
You still know when to raise your hands.
And yet there is a memory you do not want God to bring into the light.
You may have spent years telling yourself that time has made it less serious.
But time does not transform wrongdoing into righteousness.
And secrecy does not make sin disappear.
Numbers 32:23 warns:
“Be sure your sin will find you out.”

In its original context, Moses was warning certain Israelite tribes about failing to fulfill their covenant responsibilities. The words should not be treated as a promise that every hidden offense will inevitably become publicly known in this life.
Nevertheless, the warning reminds us that wrongdoing cannot be safely dismissed merely because human beings have not discovered it.
God sees what people conceal.
Hebrews 4:13 teaches that nothing in creation is hidden from His sight.
That truth can be terrifying.
But it can also become the beginning of freedom.
Because the God who sees the hidden sin is also the God who calls sinners to repentance.
And the God who sees hidden suffering does not require victims to pretend their wounds never existed.
Here is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
The Old Testament's moral seriousness does not disappear when Jesus enters the story.
Jesus did not arrive to announce that holiness had been a misunderstanding.
He did not tell humanity that sin was harmless.
He did not redefine repentance as simply feeling better about ourselves.
In Matthew 5:17, Jesus said:
“Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil.”
Christ fulfills the Law and the Prophets.

That means we must read Deuteronomy through the full unfolding of God's redemptive purposes, rather than treating every command given to ancient Israel as an unchanged legal procedure for the church today.
The church is not instructed to reenact the Mount Ebal ceremony or establish the civil penalties of ancient Israel.
But the New Testament does not treat incest as morally acceptable.
In fact, the apostle Paul confronted a shocking situation in the Corinthian church.
First Corinthians 5:1 says:
“It is reported commonly that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as is not so much as named among the Gentiles, that one should have his father's wife.”
There it is again.
A man involved sexually with his father's wife.
The same family relationship condemned in Deuteronomy 27:20.
Centuries had passed.
The covenantal administration had changed.
Christ had come.
Yet Paul did not celebrate the situation as an expression of freedom.
He confronted it.
The Greek word Paul used for sexual immorality was πορνεία (porneia), a broad term referring to illicit sexual conduct.
And what disturbed Paul was not only the reported wrongdoing.
It was the church's attitude toward it.
Rather than mourning the situation, the community had become arrogant.
Think about the implications.
A church can be spiritually proud while morally compromised.
It can have impressive gatherings and still refuse to confront destructive behavior.
It can talk endlessly about grace while forgetting that grace is never permission to continue exploiting people.
Paul instructed the church to take the matter seriously through church discipline, with the aim of confronting the offender and protecting the integrity of the community.

Later, in 2 Corinthians 2:6–8, Paul urged the Corinthians to forgive and comfort a disciplined person who had experienced sufficient correction. The passage does not explicitly identify that individual as the man from 1 Corinthians 5, so we should not claim with certainty that it records his restoration.
Still, the larger New Testament witness is clear.
Christian correction is not supposed to be an exercise in cruelty.
It is meant to uphold truth and, where genuine repentance occurs, seek restoration consistent with justice and safety.
And that brings us to the most difficult question of all.
Can someone guilty of a deeply shameful sexual sin truly be forgiven?
The Gospel answers with hope.
But not cheap hope.
Not the kind that says, “Just say sorry, and everyone must trust you again.”
Not the kind that tells a wounded person to forget what happened.
Not the kind that confuses forgiveness with avoiding consequences.
Biblical repentance involves turning away from sin.
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) means repentance, involving a changed mind and orientation that bears fruit in a changed life.
It is not merely embarrassment after being caught.
It is not sorrow because a reputation has been damaged.
It is not a carefully rehearsed apology designed to regain access to someone who has been harmed.
Genuine repentance acknowledges wrongdoing without shifting blame.
It accepts accountability.
It stops harmful behavior.
It respects boundaries.
It does not demand immediate reconciliation.
And when a crime has been committed, spiritual language must never be used to obstruct lawful reporting, investigation, or protection.
A repentant person cannot purchase forgiveness through secrecy.
Nor can repentance erase another person's right to safety.
Yet even here, in the place where guilt is undeniable, the Gospel announces something astonishing.
Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
Not to pretend sin was insignificant.
But to deal with sin through His death and resurrection.
Galatians 3:13 declares:
“Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree.”
The Greek begins:
Χριστὸς ἡμᾶς ἐξηγόρασεν ἐκ τῆς κατάρας τοῦ νόμου
Christos hēmas exēgorasen ek tēs kataras tou nomou.
“Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law.”
The word ἐξηγόρασεν (exēgorasen) communicates redemption or release by purchase.
The word κατάρα (katara) means curse.
Paul draws upon Deuteronomy 21:23 to explain the significance of Christ's crucifixion.
Notice what the apostle is saying.
The Law exposed humanity's guilt.
Christ bore the curse on behalf of those He came to redeem.
This does not mean that every specific curse pronounced in Deuteronomy 27 should be mechanically equated with a particular individual's experience.
It means that the larger reality of condemnation under the Law finds its redemptive answer in the crucified and risen Christ.
At the cross, God did not simply shrug at evil.
Sin was taken with immeasurable seriousness.
And grace was revealed with immeasurable beauty.
Imagine that.
The One who had no sin willingly gave Himself for sinners.
The One who was perfectly holy entered a world of betrayal, violence, corruption, and shame.
The One who deserved worship was mocked.
The One who gave life was put to death.
And on the third day, He rose.
Not so that humanity could return comfortably to darkness.
But so that those who believe in Him could receive forgiveness and new life.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we repaired every consequence of our past.
Not after we learned to sound religious.
Christ died for sinners.
But please do not misunderstand what this means.
The Gospel is not a shelter for unrepentant abuse.
It is not a theological loophole for those who refuse accountability.
And it is not a command for victims to surrender their safety so an offender can feel restored.
Christ's grace is free, but it is not trivial.
The Savior who forgives also calls people to follow Him.
And following Him means walking in truth.
Perhaps you are reading this as someone who has carried guilt for years.
You know what you did.
You cannot undo it.
You cannot go back and become the person you should have been.
But you can stop defending the sin.
You can confess it to God.
You can turn away from it.
You can accept appropriate accountability and seek help to ensure the harm is not repeated.
And you can come to Jesus Christ without pretending to be innocent.
First John 1:9 declares:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
That is not a promise that earthly consequences vanish.
It is a promise concerning God's forgiveness and cleansing.
And sometimes the most powerful evidence of repentance is a person's willingness to face consequences rather than escape them.
Perhaps, instead, you are reading this as someone who was harmed.
You have spent years asking why God did not stop what happened.
Why someone who claimed to love you crossed a boundary that should never have been crossed.
Why people believed the person who hurt you.
Why healing has taken so long.
I will not pretend that one article can answer every painful question.
And I will not tell you that the mere passage of time should have healed everything.
But I want you to know something.
The sin committed against you does not determine your worth.
You are not spiritually contaminated because another person violated your dignity.
You do not have to carry the offender's guilt.
And you do not have to call injustice good in order to demonstrate Christian forgiveness.
The Lord is near to the brokenhearted, as Psalm 34:18 declares.
Healing may involve prayer, trusted support, qualified counseling, appropriate reporting, and the patient rebuilding of safety.
Seeking that help is not a failure of faith.

And if you are currently being harmed, especially if you are a minor or someone dependent on the person responsible, please reach out to a safe adult, appropriate protection service, or local authorities.
Your safety matters.
Your voice matters.
Your life matters.
Now consider the deeper message of those ancient declarations.
When Israel answered “Amen,” the people were affirming that God's standards were true.
But what happens when a community says “Amen” to God's holiness in public and refuses to practice justice in private?
What happens when we condemn biblical sins on social media but protect those same sins within our circles?
What happens when a church fears scandal more than it fears disobedience?
What happens when we care more about preserving an institution's reputation than protecting someone who has been wounded?
The answer is devastating.
Our public religion becomes a contradiction of our private conduct.
Jesus confronted religious hypocrisy with piercing clarity.
In Matthew 23:27, He compared hypocritical religious leaders to beautiful whitewashed tombs that were inwardly full of uncleanness.
The image is unforgettable.
Beautiful outside.
Corrupt within.
A polished exterior cannot transform what is hidden underneath.
And this is why the Gospel Warrior message must never be reduced to an attractive slogan.
From Scandal to Grace does not mean from exposure to successful damage control.
It does not mean from wrongdoing to a restored public image without repentance.
It does not mean from victimization to enforced silence.
It means bringing what is broken, sinful, and wounded into the light of Jesus Christ.
It means allowing truth to speak.
It means calling evil what God calls evil.
It means seeking justice without surrendering to hatred.
It means offering the hope of forgiveness without excusing the wrong.
It means believing that Jesus can transform lives while recognizing that trust must be rebuilt through truth, safety, and consistent change.
And perhaps that is the word someone desperately needs today.
The Gospel does not require you to keep pretending.
You can stop hiding behind religious appearances.
You can stop defending what Scripture condemns.
You can stop believing that your worst moment is more powerful than the grace of Jesus Christ.
And if someone sinned against you, you can stop believing that their wrongdoing has the authority to define your identity.
At the cross, we encounter both the seriousness of sin and the extraordinary mercy of God.
Neither truth cancels the other.
Justice matters.
Repentance matters.
Grace matters.
And Jesus Christ is at the center of them all.
Now I want to ask you something deeply personal.
Not as a test of how religious you sound.
Not to pressure you into exposing a painful experience publicly.
But because sometimes a simple, truthful response is the beginning of an important conversation.
What part of this message spoke most deeply to you—the holiness of God, the danger of hidden sin, the need to protect the wounded, or the hope of forgiveness through Christ?
You might simply write “Christ is still healing me” if you are learning to trust Him through a painful season.
Or “No more hiding” if you are ready to turn away from sin and seek genuine accountability.
Or “Pray for me” if you need the encouragement of other believers.
You never need to disclose the details of abuse, identify an offender, or make a public confession of sensitive wrongdoing in a comment section.
But your words may remind another person that they are not alone in seeking Christ.
And if this article has opened your eyes to something Scripture teaches, please save it.
Not because saving a post earns spiritual merit.
But because there are truths worth revisiting when emotions settle and we are ready to study God's Word more deeply.

A thoughtful share may reach a friend, a family member, a struggling believer, or someone who has quietly wondered whether the Bible has anything meaningful to say about the things families refuse to discuss.

If someone comes to mind, consider tagging them only when doing so would be appropriate and respectful of their privacy. Sometimes sending the article privately with a gentle personal message is the more loving choice.
We want believers to grow beyond inspirational phrases into serious biblical understanding.
We want seekers to encounter the truth of the Gospel.
We want wounded people to hear that God's holiness does not make their suffering invisible.
And we want those trapped in sin to know that repentance and transformation are possible through Christ.
Every article takes time to study, write, refine, and share. Every effort to provide biblical teaching and discipleship resources requires continued commitment.
Not out of guilt.
And certainly not because anyone must pay us to glorify God.
But supporting faithful Christian teaching can be one meaningful expression of generosity and stewardship.
Your responsibilities to your family, your local church, and those in need matter.
Please never give beyond your means or under spiritual pressure.
And it can help us make more resources available to people who are hungry for God's Word.
Those free resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment accessible.
Those products can serve as reminders of faith, encouragement, and conversations about Jesus Christ. But the greatest purpose of this invitation is not merchandise.
It is helping more people encounter biblical truth.
It is continuing to proclaim that sin is serious, grace is real, and Jesus Christ is mighty to save.
You can still be part of this mission.
Read the Word.
Pray for the people we reach.
Help someone find a free Christian resource.
Encourage a struggling believer.
And above all, live in a way that honors Jesus Christ.
Because our ultimate goal is not to build an audience that admires a page.
It is to point people toward the Savior who deserves their hearts.
Before you leave, return with me for one final moment to the mountains of Deuteronomy.
Picture Israel standing before the solemn words of God's covenant.
The Levites speak.
The people listen.
The curses are declared.
And thousands of voices answer:
“Amen.”
Now move forward through the centuries.
Past Israel's failures.
Past the prophets' warnings.
Past generations of human rebellion and suffering.
Until you reach a hill outside Jerusalem.
Golgotha.
There, the sinless Son of God hangs upon a cross.
The crowds do not fully understand what is unfolding before them.
The disciples are shaken.
The sky grows dark.
And the One who came to redeem sinners gives His life.
The story does not end at the cross.
The tomb will be empty.
Death will be defeated.
And the risen Christ will send His followers to proclaim repentance and forgiveness of sins in His name.
This is the Gospel.
Not that evil was imaginary.
Not that guilt was insignificant.
Not that suffering did not matter.
But that God, in His mercy, provided salvation through Jesus Christ.
Deuteronomy reminds us that holiness is not negotiable.
Calvary reveals the astonishing cost of redemption.
The resurrection announces that death and sin do not have the final word over those who belong to Christ.
So whether you came to this article carrying guilt, grief, confusion, or a longing to understand God's Word, do not leave looking only at the curse.
Look to Christ.
If you have sinned, repent and turn to Him.
If you have been wounded, know that your suffering does not make you guilty of another person's wrongdoing.
If you have hidden behind religious appearances, ask God for the courage to walk in truth.
If you have mistaken grace for permission to continue in sin, hear the call of Jesus to follow Him in a transformed life.
And if you have believed your story is too ruined for redemption, remember that the Savior who rose from the grave is not defeated by the darkness of human history.
The scandal may explain what happened in your story, but it does not have to be the final word over the life you surrender to Jesus Christ.
